title: AI Data Centers Have A Power Hoarding Problem
gist: AI data centers waste most of their contracted power: redundancy schemes like 2n and three-makes-four plus 70-80% target utilization mean only about a third of a 2GW provisioned site reaches compute, according to Utilidata. Chip-level fixes (IP power states, NoC clock gating, proteanTecs guard-band reclamation) cut consumption but paradoxically worsen utilization, so the emerging play is dynamic power orchestration — millisecond DVFS/power-capping plus rack-level sensing at a million samples per second — to run redundant feeds at 95-98% and back down on failure.

themes.theme: Idle and stranded power as the dominant loss

insights.claim: Idle power is the single biggest power sink in computing systems, arising both from servers running at higher-than-necessary voltage and from power deliberately held in reserve.
insights.speaker: Arif Khan, VP of product marketing for design IP, Cadence
insights.so_what: Reframes data center efficiency spend away from peak-performance-per-watt toward idle/reserve reclamation — a different vendor set benefits.
insights.quote: Idle power is by far the biggest sink of power in systems
insights.locator: Intro — "These two issues are converging in the ongoing focus on data-center power"

insights.claim: Stranded power arises from both directions of provisioning error: over-provisioned resources strand power when planners assume all resources run near full utilization, while under-provisioned resources saturate some resources and leave others idle.
insights.speaker: Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor, Rambus
insights.so_what: Provisioning accuracy, not raw efficiency, is the lever — creates demand for workload-aware capacity forecasting tooling.
insights.quote: Over-provisioned resources can lead to stranded power if data centers plan for all resources to be at or near full utilization.
insights.locator: Intro — "Customers are talking about this more openly now"

insights.claim: Operators of large data centers are now discussing stranded power openly because small inefficiencies compound quickly at scale, marking a shift from a previously ignored topic to an active procurement concern.
insights.speaker: Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor, Rambus
insights.so_what: An emerging budget line: expect RFPs for power-utilization products where none existed a year ago.
insights.quote: Customers are talking about this more openly now, especially in large data centers where small inefficiencies add up fast
insights.locator: Intro — "Others agree, pointing to the increasing significance of idle power"

themes.theme: IP-level power architecture and the integrator's blind spot

insights.claim: Purchased IP and its interfaces are one of the biggest sources of idle power precisely because their internals are outside the integrator's control, forcing the integrator to learn and exploit whatever power-saving features the IP vendor built in.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Power-state documentation and orchestration support become a real differentiator in IP vendor selection, favoring Cadence/Synopsys-class suppliers.
insights.locator: It starts with power-saving architectures — "One of the bigger sources of idle power can be IP"

insights.claim: As interface speeds rose, high-speed IP interfaces became far more power hungry, prompting power-optimized states, power-aware transactions and multiple levels of standby that the operating system and orchestration logic must understand to exploit.
insights.speaker: Arif Khan, VP of product marketing for design IP, Cadence
insights.so_what: Software orchestration, not silicon features, is the gating factor for realizing advertised interface power savings.
insights.locator: It starts with power-saving architectures — "From an IP perspective, a lot of this has to do with which interfaces are put to sleep"

insights.claim: When multiple jobs share a system, an interface unused by one job may be in use by another, so power-down can only reach the least common denominator across all running jobs.
insights.speaker: Arif Khan, VP of product marketing for design IP, Cadence
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant scheduling structurally caps achievable power savings — a hidden cost of consolidation that single-tenant AI clusters avoid.
insights.quote: so you can power down only to the least common denominator
insights.locator: It starts with power-saving architectures — "If you are running multiple jobs on a system"

insights.claim: The AMBA bus low-power interface port provides a Q channel for simple clock gating and power-domain control and a P channel for advanced multi-state power management, with their granularity determining how many circuits can be controlled.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Concrete standard-level mechanism behind SoC power claims; granularity of Q/P channel implementation is a checkable spec detail.
insights.locator: It starts with power-saving architectures — "The AMBA bus, for example, provides a low-power interface (LPI) port"

insights.claim: Clock gating shuts down circuits while leaving power intact, whereas power gating saves more but costs significant time both to enter and to exit, making resumption latency the core trade-off in aggressive power-down.
insights.speaker: Arif Khan, VP of product marketing for design IP, Cadence
insights.so_what: Latency-sensitive inference workloads cannot use the deepest power states — limits realizable savings in serving fleets.
insights.quote: The flip side is bringing things back up and balancing the resumption time against how much power you want to trade off.
insights.locator: It starts with power-saving architectures — "There’s a need to power things down as low as possible"

insights.claim: The network-on-chip has more power impact than any other IP block because it is the backbone of the SoC, and a typical 5+5 node configuration carries ten independently gated clocks plus per-node power states negotiated over the AMBA P-channel.
insights.speaker: Ewald Liess, SVP of sales and business development, SignatureIP
insights.so_what: NoC vendors sit on an underappreciated chip-level power lever; a specific technical claim to test against competing NoC IP.
insights.quote: Ten independently gated clocks are in a typical 5+5 nodes configuration.
insights.locator: It starts with power-saving architectures — "As a NoC is the backbone of an SoC"

insights.claim: Power consumption scales with the square of the applied voltage, but the voltage a device receives is set by worst-case characterization — the combination of hardest workload, harshest environment and end-of-life degradation — conditions that rarely all occur simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Noam Brousard, VP of systems, proteanTecs
insights.so_what: The quadratic voltage-power relationship makes guard-band reclamation one of the largest single-digit-percent-to-double-digit power levers available without new silicon.
insights.quote: However, it is rare that all these circumstances happen at the same time, all the time.
insights.locator: Each chip is a special snowflake — "Power consumption scales with the square of voltage"

insights.claim: Silicon wearout, ignored by the industry for years, is now a first-order design consideration because chips must be guard-banded to meet spec on the last day of expected service, forcing a supply voltage higher than a new chip actually needs.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Every deployed fleet is paying an aging tax on day one — a structurally addressable, recurring power cost across the installed base.
insights.locator: Each chip is a special snowflake — "One example is chip aging"

insights.claim: In-circuit monitoring can measure the real-time margin to failure of logic throughout a device, letting the system reclaim unneeded guard-bands and run at significantly lower voltage, scaling voltage back up only when the stressing conditions actually appear.
insights.speaker: Noam Brousard, VP of systems, proteanTecs
insights.so_what: A software/IP-only path to fleet-wide power reduction with no fab change — directly monetizable against data center power scarcity.
insights.quote: By reclaiming these guard-bands when they are not needed, the chip runs at a significantly lower voltage while still meeting its operational requirements.
insights.locator: Each chip is a special snowflake — "We have the ability to measure in real time the actual margins to failure"

insights.claim: Running chips on low voltage margins creates a new failure mode where a sudden workload change causes an Ldi/dt dynamic voltage drop that threatens digital logic timing integrity.
insights.speaker: Noam Brousard, VP of systems, proteanTecs
insights.so_what: Aggressive power savings import reliability risk; buyers will demand protection mechanisms, expanding the attach for monitoring IP.
insights.quote: a sudden change in workload may cause a dynamic voltage drop (Ldi/dt) that may threaten digital logic timing integrity
insights.locator: Each chip is a special snowflake — "Just as reducing power can help, at times it’s necessary to raise power"

insights.claim: A built-in hardware protection mechanism can let the host system detect and mitigate a sudden margin collapse within a couple of clock cycles, typically by clock dividing or throttling while voltage is readjusted to safe levels.
insights.speaker: Noam Brousard, VP of systems, proteanTecs
insights.so_what: Cycle-scale hardware safety nets are what make undervolting deployable in production fleets — the key technical unlock to verify.
insights.locator: Each chip is a special snowflake — "ProteanTecs has a ‘safety net’ for these scenarios"

insights.claim: The highest-value use of aging monitoring is a lifetime voltage schedule: start the chip at reduced voltage to save power and boost it occasionally over the device's service life as degradation accumulates.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Turns chip telemetry into a multi-year subscription surface rather than a one-time test insertion.
insights.locator: Each chip is a special snowflake — "Even more important is the ability to monitor aging on an ongoing basis"

themes.theme: Redundancy math strands two-thirds of contracted power

insights.claim: Securing access to power is one of the biggest timing constraints on a data center operator's business, because running a new transmission line from a substation is expensive and permitting-heavy, and on-site generation also takes a long time to permit.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: Power interconnect queue position is the scarce asset in AI buildouts — anything that raises utilization of existing interconnect has outsized value.
insights.quote: Getting access to power is one of the biggest time constraints on data center operators’ business
insights.locator: The data center gets more power than it uses — "If you just wanted to run a new transmission line"

insights.claim: In a three-makes-four redundancy scheme, three 100% feeds are required and a fourth is added as backup, with all four running at 75% so the remaining three can carry full load if one fails; alternative arrangements include 4+2 (a 2n system) and n+1.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: The redundancy topology directly sets the ceiling on usable power per megawatt contracted — a first-order input to any data center capacity model.
insights.locator: The data center gets more power than it uses — "One common approach is called 3-4"

insights.claim: Nvidia recommends three-makes-four or n+1 redundancy, but most conventional legacy data centers still run a full 2n system with two incoming lines each loaded at 50%.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: Legacy 2n sites have roughly double the reclaimable headroom of Nvidia-spec AI sites — retrofit opportunity concentrates in older colo stock.
insights.quote: Nvidia recommends a three-makes-four system or an n+1 system, but most of the common old-school data centers go for a full 2n system
insights.locator: The data center gets more power than it uses — "Still, redundant power remains unused today"

insights.claim: A site provisioned for 2GW is treated by its manager as only 1GW because of 2n redundancy, and with a 70-80% utilization target within that gigawatt only about a third of the full 2GW actually reaches compute infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: Headline gigawatt announcements overstate deployable compute by roughly 3x — critical when sizing GPU demand implied by announced power deals.
insights.quote: When you look at it as a whole, they’re getting about a third of the 2GW to the compute infrastructure.
insights.locator: The data center gets more power than it uses — "A site may be provisioned for 2GW"

insights.claim: Utilities incur the full capital cost of delivering redundant data center capacity but never sell the kilowatt-hours against it, making redundancy a shared economic loss between operator and utility.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: Aligns utility and operator incentives behind dynamic redundancy — a regulatory and rate-design angle worth tracking.
insights.quote: The utility had to put in the capital cost to deliver that capacity, but they’re not selling the kilowatt-hours
insights.locator: The data center gets more power than it uses — "Still, redundant power remains unused today"

insights.claim: Naively consuming reserve power breaks failover math: in a 3+1 configuration running all feeds at 90%, losing one feed would require the surviving three to deliver 120% of provisioned capacity, so some workload must be shed.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Explains why utilization gains require orchestration, not just policy change — the technical moat for power-control vendors.
insights.locator: The data center gets more power than it uses — "If the extra available power is used in the event of a failure"

insights.claim: Adding more equipment to consume unused provisioned power is far cheaper than building a new data center or procuring additional power at an existing one.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Densification inside existing shells is the cheapest marginal compute — bullish for retrofit hardware and rack-level power gear versus greenfield construction.
insights.locator: The data center gets more power than it uses — "While additional equipment represents an additional investment"

insights.claim: Measurable electrical transients appear in the system before an outage, so a monitoring system can pre-signal flexible jobs to back down — for example cutting 20 points of utilization from 70% to reach the 50% sustainable in a 2n system.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: Predictive outage signatures are what make overloading redundant feeds insurable — the technical claim that underwrites the whole business case.
insights.quote: Before an outage, you can definitely see transients in the system that indicate the outage is coming
insights.locator: Monitoring system power — "If we know something’s coming, we give signals to the jobs"

insights.claim: The slower control loop feeds power-capacity forecasts per rack, row and data hall into the workload scheduler rather than scheduling work itself, because moving inference work requires draining in-flight requests and loading model weights onto another replica — a seconds-scale operation.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: Power-aware scheduling integrates as a signal into existing orchestration stacks — a partnership-led go-to-market, not a scheduler replacement.
insights.quote: Schedulers operate in seconds because moving inference work means draining in-flight requests and then loading model weights onto another replica.
insights.locator: Monitoring system power — "We do not schedule or unschedule work"

insights.claim: The fast control loop acts directly on servers through the DVFS signal, also known as power capping, changing power on a millisecond timeframe.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: Millisecond-scale actuation is the difference between marketing and real failover tolerance — the spec to benchmark competing offerings against.
insights.quote: We interface with the DVFS signal (also known as power capping), and so we are changing the power on the millisecond timeframe.
insights.locator: Monitoring system power — "The other control loop is directly to the server"

insights.claim: Control reaches DVFS firmware indirectly through standard server interfaces — Nvidia's management library for GPU power behavior and the baseboard management controller for server-level telemetry — while rack AC draw is measured directly at a million samples per second instead of being estimated from server-only controls.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: Direct rack-level metrology is the claimed differentiator versus server-telemetry-only approaches — a testable technical moat.
insights.quote: whereas we measure it directly at a million samples per second. That removes the guesswork.
insights.locator: Monitoring system power — "Our technology reads and acts through standard server interfaces"

insights.claim: With a dynamic power-control system, a data center could run all four redundant feeds at roughly 95% to 98% instead of 75%, and in a 2n configuration this literally doubles the available power.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: If it holds, this is the cheapest source of incremental AI compute capacity in the market — watch for pilot deployments and third-party validation.
insights.quote: We’re saying you could run on all four lines all the way up to probably 95% or 98% if you had that dynamic system.
insights.locator: Monitoring system power — "A technique like this lets the excess provisioned power be used"

themes.theme: Power control as a new attack surface

insights.claim: The ability to modulate power at scale already exists and is already on the network, because every AI data center server has a BMC that can cap its power and every GPU host exposes power limits to any sufficiently privileged process.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: Coordinated power actuation is a latent grid-scale attack vector already present in every AI facility — a regulatory and insurance risk nobody is pricing.
insights.quote: Every server in an AI data center already has a BMC that can cap its power, and every GPU host exposes power limits to any sufficiently privileged process.
insights.locator: Security becomes part of power control — "Security has been a design requirement from the start"

insights.claim: A power-orchestration control unit concentrates capability that is currently scattered and must therefore be treated as a high-value target, secured with SOC 2 compliance, IEC 62443-4-2 industrial control system certification, secure boot, a hardware root of trust, mutual authentication on every outbound interface, and an entirely on-site control loop with no internet dependency.
insights.speaker: Marissa Hummon, CTO, Utilidata
insights.so_what: IEC 62443-4-2 listing is emerging as the gating certification for anything touching data center power actuation — a barrier to entry for new entrants.
insights.quote: The ability to modulate power at scale is already there and already on the network.
insights.locator: Security becomes part of power control — "We maintain SOC 2"

insights.claim: Chip-level power savings do not reduce total data center energy draw because saving power lowers utilization, and lower utilization leaves provisioned power on the table that could instead do more work and generate more revenue.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A Jevons-style argument: do not model semiconductor efficiency gains as reducing aggregate data center power demand or utility load growth.
insights.quote: Saving power means lower utilization. Lower utilization leaves power on the table that could do more work and generate more revenue.
insights.locator: Where efficiency and utilization meet — "It’s nice to think that, by saving power in each unit"

insights.claim: The dynamic of converting every efficiency gain into more compute rather than less energy will persist until the industry runs out of additional work to do in the data center, which is not happening anytime soon — leaving physical footprint as the binding limit.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Supports a structurally long runway for data center power demand growth; the constraint migrates from power contracts to floor space and cooling.
insights.quote: This dynamic is likely to persist until we run out of additional work to do in the data center, and that’s not happening anytime soon.
insights.locator: Where efficiency and utilization meet — "Designers keep finding ways to do more with less energy"
